reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read the Hebrew ra' in these verses as calamity or adversity set against "peace" — natural judgment God sends, not the moral evil of sin.

discrepancy.connective: Dan Barker presses the objection that the God who is called love and "in whom is no darkness" nonetheless claims in Isaiah 45:7 to create evil, listing it among the traits that make the biblical God morally repugnant.

skeptic.name: Dan Barker
skeptic.work: God: The Most Unpleasant Character in All Fiction
skeptic.attribution: Dan Barker, God: The Most Unpleasant Character in All Fiction (New York: Sterling, 2016)

excerpts.excerpt_text: create evil—not moral evil (Jam 1:13), but in contrast to "peace" in the parallel clause, war, disaster (compare Psa 65:7; Amo 3:6).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the moral-evil objection: distinguishes 'evil' here as calamity/disaster opposed to 'peace', not moral evil, citing James 1:13.

excerpts.excerpt_text: "evil" is also from him; not the evil of sin; this is not to be found among the creatures God made; this is of men, though suffered by the Lord, and overruled by him for good: but the evil of punishment for sin …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States the classic malum culpae / malum paenae distinction: God is not the author of the evil of sin, only of the evil of punishment/affliction.

excerpts.excerpt_text: I send peace and war, prosperity and adversity, as Amos 3:6.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Glosses 'create evil' as adversity paralleling peace, cross-referencing Amos 3:6 — a sovereignty-over-calamity reading, not moral evil.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats Isaiah 45:7 directly, arguing 'evil' here means natural evil — affliction, adversity — and that no text sanctions the proposition that God is the author of sin.

link.title: Isaiah 45:7—Is God the author of evil?
